Add a new upload as one entry: id = the YouTube video id, format = "video" (16:9) or "short" (9:16). paper.title must match the paper's "name" in academic-publications.json to show a Video button on the Publications page. A video without a paper can have a short "note" instead. Add "section": "educational" to show a video in the Educational section (popular-science videos that are not tied to a paper) instead of Explainers / Shorts. Use section = natures-algorithms and a numeric episode for the weekly Nature's Algorithms series, section = mathematics-of-beauty with a numeric episode for The Mathematics of Beauty series, section = estimate-it with a numeric episode for the Estimate It riddle series, and section = academia-decoded with a numeric episode for the Academia Decoded series.

videos.title: 01. The Sky Postman
videos.summary: How many people are in the air right now? Pause, estimate, then break it into flights, passengers and hours: about 1.4 million.

videos.title: 02. The Clock That Counts Heartbeats
videos.summary: How many heartbeats in a lifetime? Count the zeros: about 2.7 billion, so a ten-digit counter will do.

videos.title: 03. The Well With No Shadow
videos.summary: A shadow angle of 7.2 degrees and a 5,000-stadia road: how Eratosthenes measured the Earth more than 2,000 years ago.

videos.title: 04. The Lake Warden
videos.summary: Catch, tag, catch again: estimating the fish in a lake you can't drain, checked on 50 simulated lakes.

videos.title: 05. Serial Numbers
videos.summary: Four serial numbers and the German tank problem: the statisticians said 244 tanks a month; German records showed 271.

videos.title: 06. The Library of Everyone
videos.summary: How many people have ever lived? Split history into eras: about 130 billion against the PRB's 117 billion. The living are only about 7%.

videos.title: 01. Who Pays for Science?
videos.summary: A grant is a bet on a plan, not a reward for a result. In 2025 the ERC funded 478 of 3,928 Starting Grant proposals.

videos.title: 02. Whose Name Goes First?
videos.summary: First, last, alphabetical, or 5,154 authors: how author order works, and why to agree on it on day one.

videos.title: 03. What Happens After You Click Submit?
videos.summary: Editors, unpaid reviewers and 'revise': peer review, with the submission-to-acceptance times of 66 of our own papers (median 93 days).

videos.title: 04. Why Are So Many Papers Behind Paywalls?
videos.summary: Subscriptions, open access and article processing charges, plus five legal ways to read a paywalled paper.

videos.title: 05. What Makes a Paper Good?
videos.summary: Citations, the h-index and the impact factor, what they miss, and the cat with an h-index of 11.

videos.title: 06. What a PhD Actually Looks Like
videos.summary: Year one to the defence, how to interview an advisor, and where people go after a PhD.

videos.title: 01. The Beauty of What We Cannot See
videos.summary: Ten noisy glimpses of a hidden path, and the cloud of every path that fits them. The average path is shorter than each of 2,000 sampled paths: a path nothing ever takes.

videos.title: 02. The Most Beautiful Way to Move a Million Dots
videos.summary: A million dots moved onto a star-shaped fortress by optimal transport, Monge's 1781 problem. The plan is certified within 0.273% of the cheapest possible; a random plan costs 18.7 times more.

videos.title: 03. The Shape of Nothing
videos.summary: 1,500 noisy points on two rings. Persistent homology finds the two holes from the coordinates alone, and no loop in 200 hole-free clouds lives as long.

videos.title: 04. The Geometry of Being Wrong
videos.summary: Twelve measurements and every curve that fits them. The uncertainty does not depend on the measured values, and a model that assumes a smoother world covers the truth 26% of the time instead of 95%.

videos.title: 05. The System That Explodes Before It Dies
videos.summary: A stable system, eigenvalues −1 and −2, whose energy first grows 156-fold before it decays. Stable doesn't mean calm.

videos.title: 06. If You Could Measure Only Five Things
videos.summary: Five measurements on a hidden landscape, each placed where it removes the most uncertainty. Random sampling needs eight points to do as well, and the plan never needs the measured values.

videos.title: 07. The One Connection Holding Everything Together
videos.summary: The two busiest links of a network can be cut without breaking anything. The third busiest is the only bridge: cut it and 24 nodes are cut off. One depth-first pass finds every bridge.

videos.title: 08. Why There Is No Perfect Solution
videos.summary: A million designs for two bars holding a load: 99.9% are beaten on both material and stress. What remains is the Pareto front, where nothing improves for free.

videos.title: 09. A Thousand Futures From One Decision
videos.summary: A rule of thumb against an optimal plan, over 1,000 random futures. When both face the same futures, the plan wins 78% of them and the comparison is 5.35 times more precise.

videos.title: 10. The Beauty of Almost Impossible Events
videos.summary: An event with odds of one in 1.6 billion. A million plain simulations never see it; 100,000 importance-sampling runs land within 1% of the exact value.

videos.title: 11. The Curved Universe of Probability
videos.summary: Bell curves are points in a curved space, measured by information. The shortest path between two confident curves arcs through doubt: three times wider halfway, and 38% shorter.

videos.title: 12. The Equation That Survived the Noise
videos.summary: Can sparse regression recover a pendulum's law from noisy angles? At 1% noise the exact law returns in 41 of 50 trials; at 10% only gravity survives, and impostors appear. Every result is reported.

videos.title: Itchy eyes, aching head: allergies in children with migraine
videos.summary: In the records of Israel's largest health organization from 2000 to 2023, we found 51,411 children aged 5 to 18 with migraine. About one in three (32.4%) also had at least one allergic disease, most often allergies of the eyes and nose: allergic conjunctivitis, then allergic rhinitis. Among children with eye allergies, about 65% were girls, and children with allergies were older when they first came in (a median of 15 years versus 13). A link in past records, not a cause.

paper.title: The Association Between Allergic Disorders and Migraine in the Pediatric Population: A Nationwide Cohort Study

videos.title: Can a pandemic change how many babies are born?
videos.summary: We built an epidemic model with age groups, two sexes, births and deaths, and an infection that can lower fertility through the body itself, and ran a COVID-like pandemic on the populations of ten large cities, 100 times each, over ten simulated years. When infection reduced fertility, births fell further and the effect could ripple on for generations; the decline grew almost linearly with the infection's effect on fertility. New York was hit harder than Istanbul, but the drop in births stayed secondary to the spread itself. A simulation, not a forecast.

paper.title: Modeling the effects of pandemics on physiology-related fertility decline in society

videos.title: Is this service dog stressed? Three measures, three answers
videos.summary: We followed seven young Labradors from one litter through four weeks of early service-dog training and ranked them by three welfare measures: facial movements coded with DogFACS, the stress hormone cortisol in their urine, and ratings by trainers and non-experts. Trainers' ratings matched cortisol best (Kendall's tau 0.67), non-experts close behind (0.60), but the facial ranking showed no agreement with cortisol (0.00). With seven related dogs and no comparison group, the study can't say which measure is right, only that they disagree.

paper.title: Short communications: a methodological pilot comparing facial, endocrine, and observer-based welfare measures in service dogs (Canis lupus familiaris)

videos.title: A blood-test model that's not allowed to miss
videos.summary: Children's community blood tests are often repeated within hours in the emergency department, though only 13.3% (blood counts), 16.3% (electrolytes) and 19.0% (C-reactive protein) of repeats were justified by our criteria. An off-the-shelf XGBoost model predicted when a repeat was needed with 91.8%, 89.1% and 79.2% accuracy. Set to a safety mode that never misses a needed repeat, it kept 73.9%, 67.3% and 55.4%: still enough to cut many unneeded repeats, less so for CRP. Its value in practice still needs study.

paper.title: Shall we repeat? Predicting the necessity to repeat blood testing in pediatric emergency departments of laboratory tests previously performed in the community using a machine learning model

videos.title: Test less when it's calm, more when it's not
videos.summary: Electronics factories run every test on every circuit board. Our framework finds the cheapest set of test steps that caught every past defect, then a multi-armed bandit decides board by board between the full tests and that shortcut, based on how stable production looks. On 28,000 board runs, the shortcut alone cut test time by 18.78% and 91.57% at two stages, but when production drifted it let 110 faulty boards through at the first; the adaptive policy switched back to full testing and let none through, at the cost of some savings.

paper.title: A quality-preserving model for test reduction in electronics production

videos.title: When AI suggests an antidepressant, who sets the priorities?
videos.summary: AI can predict a patient's chance of remission and of side effects for each antidepressant, but how should those odds be combined? In a prototype tested by 22 physicians on realistic cases, three versions were compared: raw probabilities, fixed expert weights, and weights the physician sets with sliders. The slider version was rated most useful and changed physicians' first choice most often (33.3% of cases); fixed expert weights changed the fewest (15.8%). An exploratory pilot with simulated cases.

paper.title: Bridging algorithmic prediction and clinical agency: an exploratory pilot study of AI-augmented physician antidepressant choice

videos.title: What if equation-finding AI could see the neighbors?
videos.summary: Symbolic regression searches for a formula that explains data, but usually treats every row of a table as independent, while in physics a point depends on its neighbors in space and time. We add a second representation, a graph whose nodes are places and moments, turned into extra features by a graph neural network that any symbolic regression tool can use unchanged. Across ten tools and ten physics equations, results improved or matched for every tool, mostly by 1 to 3%, and errors grew up to 10 to 15% more slowly with noisy data. Tested on synthetic benchmarks.

paper.title: Moving from table to graph in physics-informed spatio-temporal symbolic regression

videos.title: In septic shock, the shape of the dose curve matters
videos.summary: We reconstructed hourly noradrenaline doses for ten days in 1,111 septic shock patients in Israel and grouped the curves by shape: five patterns emerged. The same pipeline, unchanged, found six patterns with the same core shapes in 9,343 patients from a US database, and the same order of risk: 90-day mortality of 37 to 89% across patterns in Israel and 16 to 69% in the US. Time to the peak dose and drug given on days two to four mattered most, and one day of data identified the final pattern about 85% of the time. Descriptive patterns, not yet a treatment guide.

paper.title: Noradrenaline-trajectory phenotypes in septic shock: derivation and external validation in two independent cohorts

videos.title: Eczema before age 5, migraine later? What 6,839 children show
videos.summary: Among 6,839 children diagnosed with migraine between ages 5 and 18, 2,216 had an allergy recorded before age five. Eczema (atopic dermatitis) was the most common early allergy (41.7%), followed by allergic rhinitis, asthma, eye allergies and food allergies. Asthma was the only one that differed by sex, more common in boys, and most children had just one allergy. Which early allergies a child has may play a role in migraine risk, a question for future studies; these records show a link, not a mechanism.

paper.title: Allergic diseases in early childhood and their association with migraine: a large-scale retrospective study

videos.title: An ICU feeding warning sign holds up in a second country
videos.summary: A rule built in Israel spots when a critically ill body switches from breaking down to recovery, using insulin resistance and recovery signs including C-reactive protein. In a large US database, CRP was recorded in only 3.7% of stays, so we set a stricter rule without it. Across 8,732 ICU stays it found a switch in 55.4%, and heavy feeding before the switch was linked to about 1.5 times the odds of death within 90 days (1.52 crude, 1.62 adjusted, 1.54 weighted). An association that supports the idea, not proof that feeding less saves lives.

paper.title: Pre-transition nutrition dose and mortality using a CRP-Free operational metabolic transition framework: A MIMIC-IV transportability analysis

videos.title: Can an AI-built model match one tuned by hand?
videos.summary: In 2,604 patients aged 65 and over who had urgent hip fracture surgery, more than a third died within a year. Among ten hand-tuned machine learning and deep learning models, XGBoost predicted one-year mortality best (AUC 0.846). A model built automatically by a large language model with an AutoML tool nearly matched it (AUC 0.844), with higher recall and slightly lower precision; deep learning did worse on this table data. Key predictors included albumin and urea, age, low body temperature during surgery and the number of chronic diseases. One hospital, looking back.

paper.title: Comparing Manual vs. Automated Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for Predicting One-Year Mortality in Elderly Hip Fracture Patients

videos.title: Chimps copy each other's faces, not just in play
videos.summary: Rapid facial mimicry, copying another's expression within moments, has mostly been studied with play faces during play. Using videos of 18 chimpanzees at the Los Angeles Zoo across ten contexts and nine kinds of facial signals, we measured how many facial muscle movements were copied and what share. None of our three predictions held: arousal had the highest share copied (0.817, above play's 0.762), and signals with more muscle movements had more of them copied, not fewer. Mimicry may be more widespread than thought; one troop, data from an earlier project.

paper.title: Expanding the horizons of facial mimicry in chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes): new insights into diverse signal types and contexts

videos.title: ICU feeding: follow the body's clock, not the calendar
videos.summary: Critical illness puts the body in a breakdown state, and recovery begins when it switches to rebuilding, but there's no validated marker of that switch. We built one from a daily insulin resistance index. In 2,350 ICU patients, 94% made the switch, about 60% by day three; switching by day three was linked to lower 90-day mortality (hazard ratio 0.72). Heavy feeding before the switch was linked to higher mortality (odds ratio 1.25), while heavy feeding timed by calendar days showed no such pattern. One hospital's records; associations that need validation.

paper.title: Detecting the metabolic transition to personalize nutritional timing: model development and preliminary validation in a large ICU cohort

videos.title: Can chronic stress predict cancer? Only as one piece of the puzzle
videos.summary: We surveyed 1,318 adults about stress, health, background and family history; 18% had had cancer. Stress frequency, stress level and its health impact were associated with having had cancer, but stress alone predicted it only slightly better than a coin flip. Adding background and family history helped: XGBoost was right 73% of the time, with family history and age the strongest associations and stress next. A one-time self-reported survey, so cancer may also raise stress rather than the other way around.

paper.title: Chronic Stress, Immune Suppression, and Cancer Occurrence: Unveiling the Connection Using Survey Data and Predictive Models

videos.title: Can a simple formula learn from a black-box model?
videos.summary: Symbolic regression finds readable formulas but is usually less accurate than gradient boosting. We first train a gradient boosting model, the teacher, then train symbolic regression, the student, on the teacher's predictions. Across three symbolic regression tools and ten datasets, the student improved by 3.3 to 6.7%. On wildfire danger its error dropped by 3.4% over 50 runs, and it followed the teacher's logic: rain on the day lowers risk, rain in the month before can raise it. A way to explain what the black box learned; modest gains.

paper.title: Follow the Forest Trail: Distillation by Gradient Boosting Models to Enhance Symbolic Regression Performance

videos.title: Pay the whole surgical team by results: do operations get faster?
videos.summary: In Israel's public hospitals, afternoon surgical sessions are paid collectively, at the hospital level. Across 35,635 elective operations in 23 public hospitals in 2018 and 2019, the 12.78% done under this performance pay were shorter: 40.2 minutes on average versus 64.5, and the difference held in a matched sample. Patients' length of stay showed no robust overall difference and varied by hospital, better in some and worse in others. Observational data; operation time is only one measure of performance.

paper.title: The impact of collective performance-related pay on street-level bureaucrats’ performance and clients’ outcomes

videos.title: FAME: a neural network optimizer that breaks the lag
videos.summary: Popular optimizers smooth the noisy gradient with a moving average, which notices changes in trend late. FAME (Fast Adaptive Moment Estimation) uses a triple exponential moving average, which tracks trends with less lag. Tested on 22 architectures, from small convolutional networks to vision transformers, on classification, detection and segmentation, it gave the best results in 88.46% of the models' experiments and needed 23.7% fewer training epochs, at about 3% more memory and computation per epoch. Computer vision tasks only.

paper.title: Break a Lag: Triple Exponential Moving Average for Enhanced Optimization

videos.title: Under anesthesia, blood pressure falls in 5 different ways
videos.summary: With blood pressure measured every minute for ten minutes after anesthesia induction in 17,645 adults at Sheba Medical Center, a clustering algorithm found five shapes: an early dip then a plateau (31.8%), a gradual severe decline (29.6%), a gradual moderate decline (18.4%), a dip that settles low (12.7%) and a dip that recovers (7.5%). The groups differed in starting blood pressure, chronic illness and blood pressure medicines, more than in anesthetic doses. One center's records; the shapes need validation with richer clinical data.

paper.title: A time-series clustering analysis of postinduction blood pressure trajectories

videos.title: Can culling jackals make a rabies outbreak worse?
videos.summary: In Israel, golden jackals are a main carrier of rabies, fought with oral vaccine baits and culling where jackals gather. Our model of rabies spreading through a network of jackal activity centers, built with tracking data from the Harod Valley, found that vaccination reduced the outbreak on every measure, while culling often didn't: it removes vaccinated jackals too and makes survivors move more. With little vaccination, culling up to about a tenth of the population raised the spread. A model, awaiting field confirmation.

paper.title: An empirically-parameterized spatio-temporal extended-SIR model for combined dilution and vaccination mitigation for rabies outbreaks in wild jackals

videos.title: When cats face off, they get closer than when they're friendly
videos.summary: We filmed 53 adult cats at a cat rescue lounge in Los Angeles during 186 face-to-face encounters, and an AI computer-vision system estimated the distance between them. Against our prediction, cats were closer during non-friendly facial signaling than friendly. Sex mattered as predicted: two females stayed closest, then mixed pairs, and two males furthest. On average the cats were about half a meter apart, and touching was rare (0.3%). Closer doesn't always mean friendlier; one rescue lounge.

paper.title: Close encounters of the cat kind: The influence of context and sex on facial signaling proximity in domesticated cats (Felis silvestris catus)

videos.title: Are public servants kind because of who they are, or where they work?
videos.summary: Teachers, police officers and social workers decide every day how far to go for the people they serve, but real officials can't be randomly assigned to different kinds of offices. We simulated a city with 10,000 public servants and a million citizens, in traditional administration, New Public Management and the approach that came after it. The setting mattered more than personal character: under New Public Management servants were much less prosocial, and more servants per citizen made them more prosocial, though not in a straight line. A simulation, not a measurement of real officials.

paper.title: Do Institutions Make Street-Level Bureaucrats Prosocial? Agent-Based Evidence Shows That New Public Management Does Not

videos.title: Tighten the lasso: finding outliers with a convex hull
videos.summary: Wrap the data in a convex hull, like a rubber band around every point: outliers stretch it, so removing one shrinks the hull's volume far more than removing a typical point. Our method peels off points until the volume stops changing much. Against seven widely used anomaly detection methods on ten datasets it performed comparably to the state of the art, and a quick test tells in advance which datasets suit it. It struggles with ring-shaped data and is heavy to compute.

paper.title: Tighten the lasso: a convex hull volume-based anomaly detection method
paper.venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, 2025

videos.title: How do scientists read an animal's face?
videos.summary: From Darwin's 1872 descriptions to catalogues of facial signals and facial action coding systems, where experts score every muscle movement, reading animal faces has been precise but slow: a few seconds of video can take hours to code. AI is speeding this up; an automated mouse grimace scale trained on over 5,700 images detected pain with 94% accuracy. AI has limits too, from scarce labelled data to the gap between a movement and a feeling, so this overview argues for combining human expertise with machine speed.

paper.title: Faces of time: a historical overview of rapid innovations in coding animal facial signals

videos.title: What shape will a tumor grow into?
videos.summary: Partial differential equation models of cancer need assumptions about the tumor's unknown boundary. Our agent-based simulation uses individual cells with the same rates as the equations and no boundary assumptions: the edge emerges from the cells. For a spherical tumor, the simulated volume agreed better and better with the equations as repetitions increased, and the simulation produced shapes that are hard for the equations, such as an ellipsoid like ductal carcinoma and a shape like skin cancer. A simple cancer model.

paper.title: Comparing partial differential equations and agent-based simulations in spatio-temporal modeling of cancer growth and shape
paper.venue: Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics, 2025

videos.title: Could AI recommend the right surgery, and explain why?
videos.summary: We combined recommender systems with large language models to suggest surgical procedures, using the Hebrew-language records of 68,633 patients from one of Israel's largest hospitals and 17 categories covering 1,731 procedures. Language models represented the records, enriched the procedure descriptions and explained each suggestion; dedicated recommender models outperformed general machine learning. Clinicians rated the explanations highly for accuracy and ease of understanding, a little lower for clarity and completeness. Data from a single hospital.

paper.title: Explainable Surgical Procedures Recommender System Leveraging Large Language Models

videos.title: Can a 15-second video tell two fruit fly larvae apart?
videos.summary: The Mediterranean fruit fly and the peach fruit fly are major fruit pests and quarantine pests in many countries, but their larvae are practically impossible to tell apart by eye, and DNA tests are costly and slow. We filmed single larvae crawling on a Petri dish; computer vision tracked their shape as they moved. Trained on 1,306 videos and tested on 327, the model told the species apart with 90% accuracy from 15-second clips. In the lab, with fixed cameras and steady light.

paper.title: Non-Invasive Computer Vision-Based Fruit Fly Larvae Differentiation: Ceratitis capitata and Bactrocera zonata

videos.title: Does a child really need the same blood test twice in one day?
videos.summary: Children often reach the emergency department with recent community test results and are tested again within hours. In 7,813 pediatric emergency visits, only about 7 to 14% of repeats were justified: a move from normal to abnormal, or a change of at least 20%. A simple, readable decision tree predicted when a repeat was needed with 78.7% accuracy for blood counts and 73.2% for electrolytes, beating logistic regression, but barely beat chance for C-reactive protein. Retrospective data from one health organization.

paper.title: A Machine Learning-Based Guide for Repeated Laboratory Testing in Pediatric Emergency Departments

videos.title: What would a computer notice if it paid attention like us?
videos.summary: Inspired by surprisability, our instinct to focus on the unexpected, Learning via Surprisability transforms long, high-dimensional timelines by measuring how far each moment deviates from expected behavior. On sensor data with cyber attacks it had the highest AUC (82.3%, against 54.5% for Isolation Forest); on 30 years of causes of death it showed HIV deaths peaking in 2004–2005; and it traced words across 233 State of the Union addresses. Results stay interpretable, though another method had a higher F1 on the sensor data.

paper.title: Interpretable transformation and analysis of timelines through learning via surprisability

videos.title: Do police feel ready for emergencies when they trust each other?
videos.summary: We surveyed a representative national sample of 2,733 police officers in Brazil about their trust in peers, commanders and their institution, and how ready they think their organization is for emergencies. The more they trusted, at every level, the more ready they felt their organization was, and a non-linear model explained the link better than a straight line. A survey shows a link, not cause and effect, and it measured perceived readiness, not performance.

paper.title: Trust and street-level bureaucrats’ readiness for emergencies

videos.title: Could a routine blood test flag lung cancer risk?
videos.summary: Lung cancer screening mostly targets older smokers, so others at risk can be overlooked. Using records of 4,076 people, 1,428 of them with lung cancer, machine learning combined age, sex and 22 blood tests from before diagnosis. It was right 71.2% of the time (AUC 78.7%), and 73.6% for people who never smoked. Age mattered most, then red cell distribution width and creatinine, while most tests made small, variable contributions. Retrospective data from one health organization.

paper.title: A blood test-based machine learning model for predicting lung cancer risk

videos.title: The Academic Midas Touch: a habit of highly cited papers
videos.summary: Instead of totals like the h-index, the Academic Midas Touch measures the share of a scientist's papers that become highly cited soon after publication (here, at least 15 citations within three years). Across 8,468 mathematicians it correlated with popular metrics without fully aligning with them. Winners of the Fields Medal, Abel Prize or Wolf Prize had a higher Midas Touch than matched peers, while their h-index and citation counts showed no significant difference. It focuses on short-term citations.

paper.title: The Academic Midas Touch: A citation-based indicator of research excellence
paper.venue: Journal of Data and Information Science, 2025

videos.title: Should companies prepare for the next pandemic, or chase profit now?
videos.summary: Our agent-based simulation joins an epidemic, a market of supply and demand and a map of supply chains to test resilience strategies. Firms that didn't prepare did best at first, then fell close to collapse within two months of a pandemic; firms that only prepared were less affected but inefficient. The best balance depends on the pandemic and the economy when it starts, so machine learning trained on over two million simulated cases estimates it for each firm (R² 0.82). A simulation, not company data.

paper.title: Evaluating supply chain resilience during pandemic using agent-based simulation

videos.title: A pandemic during a war: who should get care first?
videos.summary: We combined an SIR epidemic model with the Lanchester model of combat, in a region where one health system treats both wounded soldiers and infected civilians. A deep reinforcement learning agent learned an admission policy that cut the death toll by around 70% compared with random allocation. The dynamics were chaotic: the best policy kept switching between soldiers and civilians based on which choice would prevent more deaths right now. A simulated scenario.

paper.title: Spatio-Temporal SIR Model of Pandemic Spread During Warfare with Optimal Dual-use Health Care System Administration using Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper.venue: Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness, 2025

videos.title: Is there such a thing as a scientific lone wolf?
videos.summary: Following 7,238 scholars in biology, computer science, psychology and philosophy across their careers, we asked how often they publish alone. How many 'lone wolves' you find depends heavily on the threshold and the field: writing 40% of one's papers alone may make a lone wolf in psychology but not in philosophy. Three typical career patterns appeared across fields, most scholars in three fields steadily solo-publish only 10 to 20% of their work, and solo-publishing showed no significant link with influence.

paper.title: How lonely or influential is the Lone Wolf? An analysis of individual scholars’ solo-authorship dynamics

videos.title: Can AI predict a blood pressure crash after anesthesia?
videos.summary: Low blood pressure right after anesthesia is induced is linked to kidney injury, heart injury and stroke. Among 20,309 adults having surgery under general anesthesia, 24.4% had mean arterial pressure below 55 mmHg within 10 minutes of induction. Machine learning predicted it with an AUC of 0.73; key predictors were blood pressure before induction, the propofol dose and beta blocker use. A retrospective study that needs prospective confirmation.

paper.title: Developing a machine learning based prediction model for postinduction hypotension
paper.venue: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing, 2025

videos.title: Do chimpanzees use their faces like gestures?
videos.summary: Combining chimpFACS muscle coding with tools from gesture research, we studied over a thousand facial signals from a troop of 18 chimpanzees at the Los Angeles Zoo, built from 27 distinct muscle movements in 356 combinations. Signals made with a call were less gesture-like, rarely goal-directed and used in fewer contexts; signals combined with head movements or hand gestures were the opposite, and more gesture-like signals involved more muscle movements. One troop, in a zoo.

paper.title: Combinatorics and complexity of chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) facial signals

videos.title: When allowances grow and work shrinks: a tipping point
videos.summary: Our differential equation model follows working people whose taxes fund public goods and the allowances of a group that stays out of the labor market, applied to allowances for ultra-Orthodox men in Israel who devote their time to Torah study. Bigger allowances raise the group's private consumption, but fewer workers then fund public goods, well-being falls, and eventually the group's own benefits shrink; past a critical allowance, public goods and well-being break down. A model of economic utility only.

paper.title: Got much, got nothing: analyzing the impact of increased special interest groups’ influence on utility

videos.title: What happens when the ground shifts under an AI model?
videos.summary: When the world changes, the patterns a model learned can drift away. Instead of one model watching for drift, we built a two-level ensemble: a population of models, each with its own drift detector, under a global model, evolved by a genetic algorithm and improved with AutoML. On synthetic datasets it significantly outperformed a single model with drift detection, especially for unknown or mixed drift, and declined only sub-linearly as drift sped up. Real-world drift may differ.

paper.title: Pulling the carpet below the learner’s feet: Genetic algorithm to learn ensemble machine learning model during concept drift

videos.title: When does a scientist's writing style settle down?
videos.summary: Using over 1.8 million full-text computer science papers, we followed how scholars' writing styles change across their careers, alongside their advisors and co-authors. Styles jump around at first, then stabilize around the 13th publication, about four years of publishing. Departures from the advisor's style settle at about the same time, and collaborations change styles most when teams are small or co-authors share a gender or field, with younger scholars especially influenceable. Computer science data only.

paper.title: A computational model for individual scholars' writing style dynamics

videos.title: Can you predict a chimpanzee's rank from how it communicates?
videos.summary: Using observations of 18 chimpanzees at the Los Angeles Zoo from 2017 to 2019, a data-driven model built with a genetic algorithm learned the troop's 2017 ranks from 931 interactions, then predicted the next two years from 2,607 more. It picked up a period of instability after the death of the troop's highest-ranking female, matching what keepers and researchers saw, and the strength of social bonds was the strongest predictor of rank. One troop.

paper.title: Predicting Social Rankings in Captive Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) Through Communicative Interactions-Based Data-Driven Model

videos.title: Can AI predict who will feel sick after surgery?
videos.summary: In the records of 35,003 adults at Sheba Medical Center, early nausea and vomiting after surgery (in the recovery room) affected 3.8% and delayed (within the first day) 18.8%. An ensemble of machine learning models predicted early cases correctly 83.6% of the time and delayed cases 74.8%, beating the next-best score, the Koivuranta score, by 13.0% and 10.4%, and relying on factors that match clinical knowledge. Retrospective data from one center.

paper.title: Predicting postoperative nausea and vomiting using machine learning: a model development and validation study

videos.title: Can we predict which lightning strikes start a wildfire?
videos.summary: Lightning fires are rarer than human-caused fires but add substantial carbon emissions and account for most of the burned area in some regions. Our global models separate the two and estimate the chance that lightning ignites a fire from weather and vegetation; XGBoost reached 91.6% accuracy and held up on a year it never saw, with rain on the day mattering most. Each fire type needs its own model, and from 2014 to 2021 the global risk of lightning-sparked fires rose by about 1% a year.

paper.title: Global lightning-ignited wildfires prediction and climate change projections based on explainable machine learning models

videos.title: Could clearing senescent cells help treat prostate cancer?
videos.summary: Senescent cells stop dividing but stay alive, releasing signals such as VEGF that help cancer. We added the senolytic fisetin to a mathematical model of metastatic prostate cancer treated with enzalutamide and cabazitaxel; the model agreed with earlier experiments, and chemotherapy and fisetin were mostly synergistic. Giving fisetin a few days after chemotherapy, in the same week, left the smallest tumor. Fisetin is not a clinical treatment yet; this is a model calibrated with animal experiments.

paper.title: Spatio-temporal model of combining ADT and chemotherapy with senolytic treatment in metastatic prostate cancer

videos.title: When should a senolytic follow chemotherapy?
videos.summary: Chemotherapy turns some cancer cells senescent, and in lung cancer these release VEGF, which grows blood vessels that feed the tumor. Our model of lung cancer treated with cyclophosphamide and the senolytic fisetin agreed with mouse experiments. In a simulated trial of four three-week cycles, giving fisetin in the same week as chemotherapy shrank tumors the most, and when repeating treatment the rest between rounds should be neither too short nor too long. A model, not a human trial.

paper.title: Spatio-Temporal Model of Combining Chemotherapy with Senolytic Treatment in Lung Cancer

videos.title: What happens when an AI model meets unfamiliar data?
videos.summary: On 15 real-world regression datasets and over 40,000 model runs, we measured how models perform on out-of-distribution data. XGBoost and random forests performed best and held up relatively well, and deep learning did surprisingly well out of distribution despite weaker in-distribution results. Adding features found by symbolic regression improved out-of-distribution predictions by 3.70% on average for machine learning models and 10.20% for deep learning. The gains vary between datasets and models.

paper.title: Machine and deep learning performance in out-of-distribution regressions

videos.title: Can AI read a cat's face from just 48 points?
videos.summary: Cat faces can be described with 48 landmarks that follow the facial muscles, but placing them by hand takes over five minutes per image. Building on our automatic landmark detector, we made fully automatic pipelines for three tasks. From the landmarks alone, head shape type was recognized with 75% accuracy and pain with 66%, on cats the system had never seen; breed did no better than chance, so deep learning on the whole image suits it better. The pain data came from just 27 cats after balancing.

paper.title: Automated landmark-based cat facial analysis and its applications

videos.title: Do friendly cats copy each other's faces?
videos.summary: We studied videos of 53 cats at a cat café in Los Angeles, with their facial movements coded by experts using CatFACS. Machine learning told friendly from unfriendly interactions with above 77% accuracy from the expert codes, and 68% from automatically detected landmarks once timing was included. New measures of rapid facial mimicry showed more mimicry in friendly interactions, and ear movements were especially likely to be copied. One cat café, and brand-new measures.

paper.title: AI for Feline Faces: A Computational Investigation of the Social Function of Domestic Cat Facial Signals

videos.title: Can pigeons carry disease between dairy farms?
videos.summary: We built a model with several pathogens spreading within cows, within pigeons and between the two, with each pigeon moving freely between exploring and returning to familiar places. Run as an agent-based simulation with field data from pigeons tracked by GPS at three Israeli cowsheds, it showed that how different individual pigeons are drastically changes the size and predictability of outbreaks, and that pathogens infecting together can hold each other back. Simulations, built on data from one region.

paper.title: Individual Variation Affects Outbreak Magnitude and Predictability in Multi-Pathogen Model of Pigeons Vising Dairy Farms

videos.title: Can coffee farmers afford to fight leaf rust?
videos.summary: We extended the SIR epidemic model into a detailed map of coffee leaf rust spreading tree by tree across a farm, with its costs and income, and simulated Colombia, where most coffee farms are small. Without directly tackling the rust, keeping any profit was impractical; even with perfect knowledge of infected trees and the weather, fighting it earned at best about 4% on the investment, and in the realistic case it is expected to lose money. Simulations for one country.

paper.title: Economical–epidemiological analysis of the coffee trees rust pandemic

videos.title: Do dating apps change how STDs spread?
videos.summary: We extended the SIS epidemic model, in which people can be infected again after recovering, to include dating app users, and ran simulations based on real-world data, a hundred runs per setting. The more people adopted dating apps at the start, the higher the reproduction number climbed, and left unmanaged, wider adoption could push a population into an outbreak. Limiting users' interactions, or asking for regular infection-free test results, can help mitigate the extra spread. A simulation model, not measured data.

paper.title: Mathematical model of dating apps’ influence on sexually transmitted diseases spread

videos.title: Can an algorithm spot trouble brewing on social media?
videos.summary: A temporal graph records who interacts with whom, and when, and catching anomalies as they emerge could flag trends, threats, outbreaks or financial shifts. We put twelve data-driven anomaly detection methods to the same test on two temporal graphs, from Twitter and Facebook, looking for unusual group interactions. The pattern was unclear: no method was reliably best, which shows the field needs new approaches for networks that never stand still. Two platforms, and a benchmark of existing methods.

paper.title: Temporal graphs anomaly emergence detection: benchmarking for social media interactions

videos.title: Could routine medical records flag lung cancer risk?
videos.summary: Automated machine learning built an ensemble of Random Forest and XGBoost models from known risk factors in routine records: age, sex, body mass index, smoking history, socioeconomic status, chronic lung diseases and family history. On 4,076 patients, 1,428 of them with lung cancer, it was 71.2% accurate overall, 74.8% for smokers and 73% for people who never smoked. Chronic lung disease mattered most overall and for smokers; for never-smokers it was BMI, age and socioeconomic status. A modest prediction that needs confirming.

paper.title: Machine learning computational model to predict lung cancer using electronic medical records

videos.title: When lung cancer spreads, where will it go?
videos.summary: Small metastases are hard to see with conventional imaging. We built a bioclinical model on a patient's own three-dimensional CT scans, combining cancer cells flowing in the bloodstream, settling in tissue and growing there, to mark the regions where metastases are most likely. Validated on real-world data from ten lung cancer patients, it predicted where metastases were located with 74% accuracy. Ten patients is a small group, so the model needs testing on many more.

paper.title: Predicting lung cancer's metastats' locations using bioclinical model

videos.title: Let equations design your model's features
videos.summary: Symbolic regression searches for formulas that fit the data; we used the formulas it finds as new features for machine learning and deep learning models. On synthetic data the error (RMSE) dropped by 34 to 86%, and on 21 real-world datasets by 4 to 11.5%, with both kinds of model improving significantly. Predicting superconducting critical temperatures based on Eliashberg theory, the error fell by more than 20%, and the formula features are readable. The gains were much larger on synthetic data.

paper.title: Symbolic regression as a feature engineering method for machine and deep learning regression tasks

videos.title: Can you tell a neural network what you already know?
videos.summary: Autoencoders compress data into a code that other models use, but developers can't easily shape it, so samples that experts know belong together may end up far apart. Our Knowledge-integrated AutoEncoder, KiAE, brings external knowledge into training and keeps the desired distances and neighborhoods between groups of samples, even when the knowledge is only partly known. On three large datasets from economics, physics and biology, against nine other models, it gave a more useful representation and the best reconstruction accuracy. Wrong knowledge hurts it.

paper.title: Knowledge-integrated autoencoder model

videos.title: Which co-authors do scholars show off on Google Scholar?
videos.summary: Scholars choose which co-authors appear on their Google Scholar profile. Analyzing a new set of 120,000 profiles across four disciplines, we found that scholars tend to favor co-authors with higher scientometrics such as citation counts, but that pull weakens as their own numbers rise. Reciprocity was central: whether a co-author lists you back goes a long way toward explaining who you list. These are patterns in who gets listed, not each scholar's reasons.

paper.title: The scientometrics and reciprocality underlying co-authorship panels in Google Scholar profiles

videos.title: How do you measure money that's never reported?
videos.summary: Many estimates of the unregistered economy rely on linear regression, which tends to overfit partial data. Our deep learning model has two phases: an autoencoder compresses the economic indicators, then an LSTM network predicts how they unfold over time. With yearly data from 122 countries from 2004 to 2014, trained on the early years and tested on the last two, it beat linear regression and the best machine learning models and generalized better across countries and periods. Estimates of the hidden economy vary a lot.

paper.title: Going a Step Deeper Down the Rabbit Hole: Deep Learning Model to Measure the Size of the Unregistered Economy

videos.title: A more accurate matrix exponential for stiff problems
videos.summary: The matrix exponential solves systems of linear differential equations, and stiff matrices make it hard to compute accurately. Our algorithm builds on Putzer's method, solving its coefficient equations analytically and then approximating them. On seven kinds of stiff matrices from 3×3 to 1000×1000 it was more accurate than other algorithms at several sizes, with costs growing at about the same rate. A decision tree, built with machine learning and genetic programming, picks an efficient algorithm for each matrix, since no single algorithm wins everywhere.

paper.title: More Numerically Accurate Algorithm for Stiff Matrix Exponential

videos.title: A plant disease is coming. How should farmers seed the field?
videos.summary: Farmers can't stop a plant pathogen, but they can choose where to put each plant. We joined a spatial SIR model of the plants with a non-linear economic model of the field's output, and built an algorithm that finds the most profitable grid pattern for seeding. The strategy brought a significant economic benefit; the recovery rate and the basic infection rate mattered about equally for profit, and a bigger farm did not promise a bigger profit. A mathematical model with simulated fields, not a field trial.

paper.title: Cost-optimal Seeding Strategy During a Botanical Pandemic in Domesticated Fields

videos.title: If your data shifts, will your model pick the same features?
videos.summary: Stable feature selection means more reliable models, clearer explanations and less exposure to attacks, but common stability definitions miss resilience to data drift and unevenly missing values. We proposed a new definition inspired by Lyapunov stability: small changes to the data should cause only small changes to the selected features. Across 90 datasets it was statistically different from the classic record-stability measure, and we describe three scenarios, each best suited to one of three measures. There's no single best measure.

paper.title: A new definition for feature selection stability analysis
paper.venue: Annals of Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, 2024

videos.title: What really makes a shelter dog's life better?
videos.summary: For four weeks a small telemetry device under the skin recorded heart rate, muscle activity and body temperature in eight male dogs living long-term in an Italian shelter, with a different enrichment each week: toys and objects, the company of female dogs, or a person. New welfare indicators measured changes from a baseline day, sleep quality and day-night rhythms. All three enrichments improved welfare, individual dogs varied a lot, and the company of female dogs worked best for sleep and daily rhythms. Eight dogs in one shelter.

paper.title: Environmental enrichments and data-driven welfare indicators for sheltered dogs using telemetric physiological measures and signal processing

videos.title: Can AI understand a cow's distress calls?
videos.summary: Cows make low, closed-mouth calls for close contact and high, open-mouth calls for long distances, largely linked to negative states. We recorded twenty dairy cows during short visual isolation from the herd: 1,144 calls after removing noise, the largest such dataset so far. A deep learning system and an explainable machine learning system told low from high calls with 87.2% and 89.4% accuracy, and recognized which cow was calling with 68.9% and 72.5%. Twenty cows of one breed, in one negative situation.

paper.title: BovineTalk: machine learning for vocalization analysis of dairy cattle under the negative affective state of isolation

videos.title: Why does a sinking particle stall in denser water?
videos.summary: We tracked many particles settling through layers of different density, and machine learning searched our data, together with an earlier experiment's, for what controls the delay time: how long a particle takes, after leaving the boundary layer, to reach a steady speed. It depended strongly on six dimensionless numbers; the Reynolds and Froude numbers were correlated in our experiments, and the best symbolic-regression formula uses the Froude number alone. Trajectories fell into three types. The formula holds within the range of these experiments.

paper.title: Improved prediction of settling behavior of solid particles through machine learning analysis of experimental retention time data

videos.title: Can a model be both accurate and easy to explain?
videos.summary: Feature ensembles combine many feature selection runs, but existing algorithms don't treat explainability as a key factor. OFEE intersects feature sets to balance explainability and performance, with no parameters to tune. Measuring explainability by how small and how stable the feature set is, across nine canonical datasets it beat other feature selection algorithms on average by more than 8% on size and more than 7% on stability. Nine datasets, and two of many possible ways to measure explainability.

paper.title: An algorithm to optimize explainability using feature ensembles

videos.title: Should countries close their borders in a pandemic?
videos.summary: We joined an epidemic model that includes tourist travel with an economic model, then let multi-agent reinforcement learning search for each country's best border policy in a simulation of European countries. Keeping every border open was the worst choice, with the most infections and the least tourism revenue. The strict closures countries really used were simple and immediate but significantly worse than the optimized policy, which looked 14 days ahead. The model is not tied to any one disease.

paper.title: A Hybrid Mathematical Model for Optimal Border Closure Policy during Pandemic
paper.venue: International Journal of Applied Mathematics and Computer Science, 2023

videos.title: Can a computer judge how a dog reacts to a stranger?
videos.summary: We filmed 53 dogs during part of a stranger test and turned each dog's movement into a path. Without being told anything about the dogs, clustering split them into two main groups, relaxed dogs and dogs reacting excessively, and the groups differed in how fearful of strangers their owners rated them. A machine learning model matched the experts' coping-style scores with 78% accuracy. An exploratory study with few dogs.

paper.title: Digitally-enhanced dog behavioral testing

videos.title: Can sensor data spot a hoof infection before cows limp?
videos.summary: Each cow wore an ear-tag sensor recording its activity, eating, rumination and ear temperature. Comparing 21 cows that developed digital dermatitis, a contagious hoof infection, with 21 healthy cows, automated machine learning detected the disease on the day the first signs appeared with 79% accuracy, and predicted it two days earlier, before any signs, with 64% accuracy. One farm and 42 cows, and an early warning is not a diagnosis.

paper.title: Machine learning approaches to predict and detect early-onset of digital dermatitis in dairy cows using sensor data

videos.title: Can AI hear when a pug struggles to breathe?
videos.summary: We recorded flat-faced dogs' breathing with an electronic stethoscope during a 15-minute treadmill test, 366 recordings in all. Machine learning told dogs with BOAS (brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome) from healthy ones by sound alone, with a peak accuracy of 85% in Pugs; from recordings at rest it reached 68% in Pugs and 65% across breeds. The best results came from subsets of the Pug data, and it is not yet a diagnostic tool.

paper.title: BrachySound: machine learning based assessment of respiratory sounds in dogs

videos.title: Who would police officers risk their lives for?
videos.summary: We surveyed 2,733 police officers and detectives across Brazil. Most said they were expected to risk their lives every day (72.7%), and machine learning linked this willingness to trust in colleagues, managers and the police institution. On a 1–6 scale they were most willing to risk their lives for children (5.56), colleagues (5.40) and the elderly (5.14), and less for men, the homeless and LGBTQ+ people (4.55–4.58). Self-reports from one country; links, not causes.

paper.title: Trust and Street-Level Bureaucrats’ Willingness to Risk Their Lives for Others: The Case of Brazilian Law Enforcement
paper.venue: The American Review of Public Administration, 2023

videos.title: A pandemic in the wild is never about one species
videos.summary: We combined the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with the SIR infection model to follow many species and many strains on a food-web network, with avian influenza as the example. In simulations, more species, more strains and more infection passing between species all made ecosystems less stable on average. In a wild farm and a near-shore ocean, higher infection rates destabilised the ecosystem non-linearly, and the farm was the more stable of the two. Simulations, checked against known ecological findings.

paper.title: Multi-species prey–predator dynamics during a multi-strain pandemic

videos.title: How does a locust swarm move without crashing?
videos.summary: In our simulation each agent sees only its surroundings and learns how to move over generations, adding to the group's shared knowledge. In a swarm of 30 locusts moving on the ground, the learned swarm moved together almost as well as a model trained only to flock (0.70 vs 0.75) but avoided collisions far better (0.74, against 0.17 for the flock-only model). Even hundreds of simple rules captured only 93% of the behaviour. A flat, two-dimensional simulation.

paper.title: Collective evolution learning model for vision-based collective motion with collision avoidance

videos.title: Can we forecast a city's taxes by simulating everyone?
videos.summary: We simulated an economy from the bottom up: every consumer and every business, each deciding how to act with a genetic algorithm. For Klin, a small city near Moscow with 50 businesses and about 62,000 consumers, fitted on one year of data, the model estimated the next four years of tax revenue with an average error of 5.44%. A standard regression forecast would be expected to miss by about 11%; that comparison is an estimate, not a head-to-head test.

paper.title: Microfounded tax revenue forecast model with heterogeneous population and genetic algorithm approach

videos.title: Make AutoML 76% faster by using less data
videos.summary: AutoML tools search among millions of pipelines, and every try is slower on big data. SubStrat shrinks the data instead: a genetic algorithm finds a small subset that keeps the full data's entropy, the AutoML tool runs on it, and a short run on the full data fine-tunes the result. Across 18 datasets and three AutoML tools it cut computation time by 76.3% on average while keeping 95.85% of the best model's accuracy.

paper.title: SubStrat: A Subset-Based Optimization Strategy for Faster AutoML

videos.title: Can fake eye scans help AI diagnose rare eye diseases?
videos.summary: Some inherited retinal diseases are ten times rarer than others, so AI that suggests the gene from a retinal scan favours the common ones. SynthEye generates realistic retinal scans for 36 genetic diseases, built on 15,692 real scans from Moorfields Eye Hospital; eye doctors spotted only 47% of them as fake. Balancing the training data with synthetic scans didn't improve the diagnosis, but a model trained on synthetic scans alone did about as well as one trained on real scans.

paper.title: SynthEye: Investigating the Impact of Synthetic Data on Artificial Intelligence assisted Gene Diagnosis of Inherited Retinal Disease

videos.title: Synthetic DNA inspired by how cancer mutates
videos.summary: Our model, CGMM, borrows an idea from cancer: it takes ordinary, easy-to-find genomes and mutates them step by step until they carry a desired trait, combining a genetic algorithm with deep learning. A clustering test checked whether each converted genome grouped with real genomes of the target group: 78% passed in one ancestry test, against 57% for the best other generator, and 47% against 37% for skin melanoma. The datasets held only a few hundred genomes.

paper.title: Cancer-inspired genomics mapper model for the generation of synthetic DNA sequences with desired genomics signatures

videos.title: Can AI plan hospital staff and beds better than people?
videos.summary: We built a simulated hospital with patients, staff, beds, machines and drugs on a budget, and a deep reinforcement learning agent learned to allocate them over 10,000 simulated cases generated from the real records of four clinics in Israel. Tested on the real records, its plans would have treated patients more successfully at all four clinics, about 4.2% better on average. It is a simulation that ignores sick days, changing prices and most employment laws.

paper.title: Data-driven hospitals staff and resources allocation using agent-based simulation and deep reinforcement learning

videos.title: Can AutoML do an economist's number crunching?
videos.summary: We compared two biology-inspired AutoML tools, two other AutoML tools and two traditional methods on 50 real economic datasets, each confirmed as economic by three independent economists. Every AutoML tool beat the traditional methods on 73% of the datasets, and at least one did on 87%. On held-out test data the bio-inspired tools reached R² = 0.72, the other AutoML tools 0.70 and the traditional methods 0.58. Mostly regression tasks, with no data preprocessing.

paper.title: Benchmarking Biologically-Inspired Automatic Machine Learning for Economic Tasks

videos.title: Could BCG treat type 1 diabetes? The full model
videos.summary: The first mathematical model of how the tuberculosis vaccine BCG might treat type 1 diabetes, following BCG, macrophages, dendritic cells, the attacking T cells, beta cells and glucose in four groups of mice. For diabetic mice that ate healthily, BCG brought glucose back to non-diabetic levels; diet mattered about a hundred times more than metabolism over the short to medium term, and BCG eased the disease without eliminating it. A simplified model, based on mice.

paper.title: Mathematical Model for the BCG-based Treatment Of Type 1 Diabetes
paper.venue: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications, 2023

videos.title: Which pandemic models should we trust?
videos.summary: Most epidemic models extend SIR. This review maps how they grow, adding biology, clinics, economics, behaviour and space, and the three steps to a real tool: an efficient definition, software, and fitting to past data. Where people are and how they move is critical for airborne diseases. Equation solvers scale to whole countries, agent-based simulations suit highly realistic models or smaller populations, and the two can give very different predictions.

paper.title: Computational Applications of Extended SIR Models: A Review Focused on Airborne Pandemics

videos.title: Pick feature selection methods together, not one at a time
videos.summary: Often two feature selection methods run in a row, a filter and then an embedded method, and we argue they should be chosen together. FSPL learns from past datasets which pipeline suits a new one, searching with a genetic algorithm. On 90 classification datasets with 24 possible pipelines, no single pipeline was best everywhere; FSPL picked the best one for about half of the datasets and improved accuracy by up to 5.98% over the next best meta-learning method.

paper.title: FSPL: A Meta-Learning Approach for a Filter and Embedded Feature Selection Pipeline
paper.venue: International Journal of Applied Mathematics and Computer Science, 2023

videos.title: Should cancer immunotherapy follow a personal schedule?
videos.summary: Bladder cancer immunotherapy usually gives BCG and IL-2 once a week, the same for every patient. Using the most extensive equation-based model of BCG treatment to date, we trained deep learning to choose the timing and dose of each injection for each patient. The personalised planner left the fewest cancer cells (normalised scores as low as 0.18, against 0.42 for the weekly schedule), with gaps from under a day to over a week and eight or nine injections instead of six.

paper.title: Scheduling BCG and IL-2 Injections for Bladder Cancer Immunotherapy Treatment

videos.title: Prune a decision tree without losing accuracy
videos.summary: Pruning shrinks a decision tree but usually costs accuracy, which in medicine may be unacceptable. SAT-PP turns the tree's paths into Boolean satisfiability constraints and simplifies them one outcome class at a time, keeping the unpruned tree's accuracy. On breast, lung and cervical cancer datasets, accuracy and F1 score matched the unpruned trees exactly while query time fell by 6.8% on average. Three small datasets, and for random forests the speed-up wasn't significant.

paper.title: Decision tree post-pruning without loss of accuracy using the SAT-PP algorithm with an empirical evaluation on clinical data

videos.title: Which pandemic policy protects the economy best?
videos.summary: We linked epidemic, social and economic models through the network of what each industry buys from the others, simulated a COVID-like outbreak and tested work capsules, working from home, vaccination and industry closure. With 12% of the workforce at home, output loss fell by 1.4 percentage points; as a single policy, vaccination cut losses the most, and in combination it was about 4.5 times more effective than working from home. Simulations, and the best mix depends on each economy.

paper.title: Intervention Policy Influence on the Effect of Epidemiological Crisis on Industry-Level Production Through Input-Output Networks

videos.title: Can machine learning measure the hidden economy?
videos.summary: One way to estimate the hidden economy looks at cash use beyond what the official economy explains. We replaced the usual linear regression with a random forest and applied it to Israel with yearly data from 1995 to 2019. Trained on earlier years and tested on later ones, it predicted cash demand more accurately than two existing models, spreading its weight across 18 economic indicators instead of 12. Just 25 yearly data points, so the results need confirming.

paper.title: Implementing Machine Learning Methods in Estimating the Size of the Non-observed Economy

videos.title: Are we ready to pay for the next pandemic?
videos.summary: We propose a small dedicated income tax that fills a reserve budget, and a reserve program that moves people out of work in non-essential jobs into essential ones during a crisis. In a hundred-year simulation based on Israeli data, with an outbreak every 16 to 18 years, a tax of about 3% of the existing income tax and reserve pay of 80% of salary prevented a prolonged crisis, kept the budget out of deficit and kept output relatively high. A simplified economy.

paper.title: Financing and managing epidemiological-economic crises: Are we ready for another outbreak?

videos.title: What did COVID lockdowns do to our minds and homes?
videos.summary: We combined daily Israeli data on COVID cases, chats with an emotional support service and welfare ministry reports. In 2020 the service held 75% more chats than in 2019, and welfare records rose by 69%. Chats about loneliness, depression, anxiety, family difficulties and sexual trauma all rose, and emergency and domestic violence reports rose with the cases and further in lockdown. A model without lockdowns pointed to lockdown as a critical factor. Data from one country.

paper.title: The Causal Role of Lockdowns in COVID-19: Conclusions From Daily Epidemiological, Psychological, and Sociological Data

videos.title: Can the physics of heat bound a pandemic?
videos.summary: Models like SIR need infection and recovery rates that take time to measure, so we treated a pandemic on a social network like heat spreading through a material, which gives a worst-case and a mean-case bound. On a real social network of about 4,000 people, the worst-case bound ran about 20 times faster than the simulated epidemic and the mean-case bound about 1.7 times. Early on, use the bounds; once data arrive, switch to a full SIR model.

paper.title: Bounding Pandemic Spread By Heat Spread

videos.title: Can social media warn of the next epidemic wave?
videos.summary: We built EMIT, an AI tool that follows how much people post about COVID, flu and vaccines alongside official case numbers. Trained on US data from December 2019 to April 2021, it predicts whether a new wave will start two weeks ahead, with an AUC of 0.909. In simulated online campaigns for masks, distancing and vaccines, earlier warnings helped more, and choosing whom to reach by their connections beat reaching random people. English posts and US data only; people who never post are invisible to it.

paper.title: Early Detection and Control of the Next Epidemic Wave Using Health Communications: Development of an Artificial Intelligence-Based Tool and Its Validation on COVID-19 Data from the US
paper.venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 2022

videos.title: Smart checkpoints vs an epidemic: placement is everything
videos.summary: Inspired by security games, we placed inspection units on a town's street network to test people as they pass and isolate anyone caught infected. In influenza A simulations on 1,000 synthetic towns and a real industrial area in Israel, more checkpoints meant less spread, with diminishing returns. Placement mattered most: at half coverage, random placement didn't stop the outbreak, while a smart placement of the same units kept it under control with eight times fewer infections. Everyone is assumed biologically alike, and the approach suits small areas such as buildings, not whole cities.

paper.title: A Security Games Inspired Approach for Distributed Control of Pandemic Spread

videos.title: Whose samples should we sequence to catch a new variant?
videos.summary: Our model joins the epidemic, the virus's mutating genome and the economy, in a simulated town of 10,000 people. Sequencing nobody let a big wave run, sequencing everyone ended it fast at a huge cost, and testing a random 5% kept it in check but with waves; unplanned testing could even do more economic harm than none. An AI model that picks who to test, and how many, cut both the spread and the cost, and the cheapest and healthiest policies turned out close. A small simulated town, with no variants arriving from abroad.

paper.title: Economic aspects of the detection of new strains in a multi-strain epidemiological–mathematical model

videos.title: Live, recorded, or recorded live? Three online class formats
videos.summary: We taught the same two mathematics lessons to 168 life science students as a live online class, a recording, and a recording of the live class with classmates' questions. Students randomly assigned to the recording of the live class scored highest on the follow-up exam (47.6, vs 39.7 for live and 39.3 for the plain recording). When students could choose, those with higher past grades picked the live lesson, and 88% said being able to rewind mattered. One course, two lessons, one university, and a take-home exam.

paper.title: A distinction of three online learning pedagogic paradigms

videos.title: What does an acidifying ocean do to sharks?
videos.summary: We screened over a thousand papers and analysed 58 experiments, adding bony fish because data on sharks is scarce. Most tested the acidity expected by 2100 (pH about 7.8), and 79% of the fish experiments found harmful effects of higher carbon dioxide. In sharks it dulled senses such as smell and changed hunting and swimming, though sharks showed some resilience and effects varied between species. Every shark study was on bottom-dwelling species and most were short, so the long-term impact is still unknown.

paper.title: A Systematic Review of the Behavioural Changes and Physiological Adjustments of Elasmobranchs and Teleost’s to Ocean Acidification with a Focus on Sharks

videos.title: How do you forecast a virus that keeps mutating?
videos.summary: Most pandemic models assume a single virus, so we built SIVRI, which follows infection, vaccination, recovery and reinfection across several variants, with lockdowns built in. Fitted to Israel from March 2020 (four variants, a vaccine rollout and lockdowns), it predicted the reproduction number two months ahead with a correlation of 0.918. It had the lowest average error against a classic SIRS model and an XGBoost model, though XGBoost was slightly better in two of five test periods. One country, and gaps in testing data aren't corrected yet.

paper.title: Advanced Muti-Mutation with Intervention Policies Pandemic Model

videos.title: Could the BCG vaccine help with type 1 diabetes?
videos.summary: A conference abstract on a model of what the tuberculosis vaccine BCG does inside the body: immune cells, the T cells that attack insulin-making beta cells, the beta cells and glucose. With results obtained for mice, BCG brought glucose in patients with healthy eating habits down to the levels of people without diabetes, and diet shaped how the disease progressed. Glucose stayed steady only with repeated doses, so BCG eased the disease without curing it; a fuller model followed in our 2023 paper.

paper.title: Mathematical Model for the BCG-based Treatment of Type 1 Diabetes
paper.venue: Dynamical Systems Applied to Biology and Natural Science (abstract), 2022

videos.title: Why a bladder's shape matters in BCG cancer therapy
videos.summary: Doctors have treated bladder cancer with BCG, a weakened tuberculosis bacterium, for over forty years, but earlier models only counted the cells involved. We built the first model that also tracks where they are, with partial differential equations in a bladder drawn as a hollow ball. Early in treatment the shape-aware and count-only models differed about a hundredfold, and the shape-aware one fit earlier observations better; after about five weeks they agreed again. A model with parameters from published lab, mouse and human data, not a clinical trial.

paper.title: Treatment of Bladder Cancer Using BCG Immunotherapy: PDE Modeling

videos.title: Too little or too much? The BCG dose window
videos.summary: We simulated BCG therapy for bladder cancer with a model that follows bacteria, immune cells and tumor cells as they spread through the bladder. Too little BCG shrank the tumor slowly, sometimes not all the way; much more made the immune response spike around the end of the first week. In the model, BCG under 60,000 cells barely had any effect, while with cancer at 10% of cells or less, 80,000 cleared it in nine out of ten simulated cases over eight to ten weeks. A model, not a dosing guide; the full text is the 2019 paper.

paper.title: PDE Modeling of Bladder Cancer Treatment Using BCG Immunotherapy

videos.title: Does tumor depth change the right BCG dose?
videos.summary: We modeled BCG immunotherapy with the bladder lining split into eight layers and tracked where the cancer starts. Treatment only starts to bite once BCG reaches the deepest layer holding cancer, so deeper tumors needed more BCG in the first week: from about 1.07 million cells for the top layer to about 5 million for the deepest. The model also gives a minimum treatment time (ten weeks for one example patient), and after about ten weeks the starting depth stops mattering. A model of an average patient, not a clinical trial.

paper.title: PDE based geometry model for BCG immunotherapy of bladder cancer

videos.title: A bladder isn't a ball: shape changed the dose
videos.summary: Our earlier BCG therapy model drew the bladder as a hollow ball, so we stretched it into an ellipsoid with measured bladder proportions and reran the simulations. For tumors in the shallowest layer, the new shape called for almost twice as much BCG in the first week (1.91 vs 1.07 million cells); in the deepest layer the two shapes nearly agree. Across tumor layouts the average successful treatment came out about 80% higher. There is no public patient data yet to test this, and real bladders change shape as they fill and empty.

paper.title: Improved Geometric Configuration for the Bladder Cancer BCG-Based Immunotherapy Treatment Model
paper.venue: International Symposium on Mathematical and Computational Oncology, 2021

videos.title: Could masks alone have stopped COVID-19?
videos.summary: We simulated a population moving between home, work and school, with children and adults, with and without symptoms. Fitted to September 2020, it followed October's daily reproduction number in the US, UK and Russia with fair accuracy (MSE 0.056, 0.099 and 0.047). Under US conditions, holding the outbreak back with masks alone took more than 60% of adults in N95 masks at work, or more than 89% in disposable ones, which is unlikely in real life. A simulation fitted to one month of data.

paper.title: Pandemic Management by a Spatio-temporal Mathematical Model
paper.venue: International Journal of Nonlinear Sciences and Numerical Simulation, 2021

videos.title: Every lockdown sends two bills
videos.summary: A conference abstract on a COVID-19 model that weighs epidemiology and economics together. Instead of treating everyone alike, it splits people by age, susceptibility, symptom severity, social contacts and work status, and moves them through a network of places, so non-drug measures can be tested along with the economic losses they cause. It was checked against a month of data in three countries and released as open-source software; the full model is in our 2021 IJNSNS paper.

paper.title: Epidemiological-Economical Pandemic Management By A Spatio-Temporal Mathematical Model
paper.venue: Dynamical Systems Applied to Biology and Natural Science (abstract), 2021

videos.title: Shorter days or lockdowns?
videos.summary: We modeled COVID-19 and Israel's economy together, including jobs lost to the crisis rather than to illness. Shorter days (7.5 work hours, 4.5 school hours) prevented an outbreak, kept output highest and held deaths near 0.48%; partial lockdowns of 89% of children and 63% of adults cut deaths to about 0.21%, also with no outbreak. Locking children down was about 30 times cheaper for the economy than locking down adults, and with equal weights both measures were too harsh economically. Numbers fit Israel in 2020; parents staying home aren't modeled.

paper.title: Spatio-Temporal influence of Non-Pharmaceutical interventions policies on pandemic dynamics and the economy: the case of COVID-19

videos.title: Nobody is average: why pandemic models fall short
videos.summary: A commentary reviewing the models used to plan non-drug measures against COVID-19 before vaccines. The classic SIR model treats everyone alike; better models add age, severity, places and networks, each layer making predictions more accurate but hungrier for data, which is scarce early in a pandemic, when acting fast matters most. Infection-only models also miss how social, economic and political life changes behaviour. The argument: models should follow individuals through space and time. A position piece, not new results.

paper.title: Optimal Intervention Policies for the COVID-19 Pandemic Emerge from Socioeconomic-Heterogeneous Dynamics

videos.title: Could a longer school day have slowed COVID-19?
videos.summary: In September 2020 Israel reopened its schools with short school days, and cases rose. Our hybrid model, equations for children and adults plus an hour-by-hour simulation of who meets whom, matched Israel's data over two weeks (MSE 0.205). In the model, closing schools alone didn't stop an outbreak, while locking down half of the adults did, and longer days at school and work lowered the spread up to a point. Nine-hour school days gave a reproduction number of 1.45, against 2.28 for the policy used. A simplified model.

paper.title: The signature features of COVID-19 pandemic in a hybrid mathematical model - implications for optimal work-school lockdown policy

videos.title: How does an epidemic end?
videos.summary: Our extended SIR model splits children, adults and the elderly into five states: fifteen linked nonlinear equations. The classic way to find its stable end states leads to a fifteenth-degree polynomial and checking each state by hand. Rewriting the epidemic as a Markov chain, and using two facts (the dead stay dead, and the population stays constant), we found every stable ending for any start and any parameters: the survivors and the dead in each age group. A methods paper; spatial movement isn't modeled yet.

paper.title: Novel Method to Analytically Obtain the Asymptotic Stable Equilibria States of Extended SIR-Type Epidemiological Models

videos.title: What makes viewers side with a climate video?
